name: Castor Grey
lede: Castor Grey is a true neutral, olive-leaning grey from Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, common in the archive as a shadow and underpainting tone.

sections.title: A neutral grey from 1912
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color dates the name to 1912, at plate 31, column C, chip 2, hex #54534D [1]. The ISCC-NBS committee's 1955 match places it among the "dark greenish gray" names, 2.6 units away[1]. Its Munsell notation is recorded simply as N 3.5, a dark neutral with no measurable hue, confirming how close to true grey it sits [1]. Whether the name recalls castor, the Latin word for beaver, is not explained in the sources consulted here, and is undocumented [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[pelican|Pelican]], about three units away and barely distinguishable on screen [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of Castor Grey covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 2,735 of 23,781 paintings, about 11.5 per cent, as photographed [2]. It peaks in paintings from the 1270s, and Frederic Remington and the Danish painter Erik Pauelsen carry it well above the archive average, each more than four and a half times the base rate [2]. Its earliest appearance is a *Still Life with Plums* attributed to the early 1600s [2]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors [2].

questions.q: What does Castor Grey's Munsell notation, N 3.5, tell us about the color?
choices: It has almost no measurable hue, a true neutral
It is a very bright color
It is a named pigment, not a dictionary entry
It only exists in RAL's industrial standard
questions.answer: It has almost no measurable hue, a true neutral

questions.q: True or false: our sources confirm Castor Grey is named after castor, the Latin word for beaver.

openers: Castor Grey's Munsell notation carries no hue at all; it is about as neutral as grey gets.
